proposals.heading: One mesh, visibly different Actors
proposals.why: The source explicitly identifies the three cubes as Actors using the same mesh with different materials. This makes the relationship concrete before the abstract reference arrows.
proposals.edit: Keep the title and question. Show the full three-cube image first, then reveal the existing shared-asset diagram. Keep the material override distinct from modifying the shared mesh; do not imply the existing two-node schematic describes the exact three pictured Actors.
proposals.layout: Wide image across roughly 70% of the content area; a click reveal switches to the existing diagram. Preserve original proportions. Use an external caption: “Same mesh; per-Actor materials.”
proposals.script: These three Actors use the same mesh. What differs in their appearance? Now trace the references in our diagram. Before changing a material, identify whether you are editing the shared asset or an override on a particular component.
proposals.limit: An official documentation example, separate from the course fixture. The current page is labeled UE 5.8; no claim that its pictured UI is the classroom build. The static image is sufficient for this conceptual comparison.
proposals.title: Shared asset, separate placements

proposals.heading: What a component-level material change looks like
proposals.why: The short source animation changes the right cube’s material while the other cubes remain visually stable. It is closely related to the current Material Setup task.
proposals.edit: Keep the practice-tool screenshot, code behavior, PRACTICE MODE label and timing. Add a named “See a material override” link to the companion media. Use it only if students need to see the visual target of the practice operation.
proposals.layout: 9.16-second original GIF, shown large in the companion review. Keep the full editor frame; play once, then return to the actual practice plan. No new slide or extra lecture block.
proposals.script: This separate Unreal example shows a material override on one Actor. Our practice panel proposes a related kind of assignment, but it does not perform this engine operation. Which object should change, and what must remain unchanged?
proposals.limit: Do not present the clip as execution of the course Python tool, a newly created material instance, or proof of Undo. It depicts a manual assignment in a separate scene.
proposals.title: Material Setup: a reviewed change

proposals.heading: A design tool can let the intended result go wrong
proposals.why: NN/g’s published print-design examples contrast a warning about content outside the printable area with an interface that leaves the consequence unclear. This is a real visual-authoring task rather than a machine metaphor.
proposals.edit: Keep the title and UI/UX definitions. Show the two full screenshots on a reveal; keep the existing assessment question and connect it back to the renamer. Replace the earlier proposed crate-delivery illustration with this sourced comparison.
proposals.layout: Two equal-size images, labeled Vistaprint and Zazzle in editable slide text. Identify them as separate products, not a matched before/after. Use a large image reveal if text is too small alongside the definitions.
proposals.script: The text extends past the printable area. Which view helps you predict the consequence? Now return to the renamer: what result did the artist intend, and what evidence would establish it?
proposals.limit: Historical examples published in 2023, not an assessment of the products today. The pictures show interface feedback, not a purchased physical output. Preserve that distinction.
proposals.title: Interface and experience

proposals.heading: An artist judging the prop in context
proposals.why: No inspected online visual closely matched the slide’s specific user story. Reimport settings, generic developer photos and older Datasmith demonstrations change the focus. One bespoke illustration fills the conceptual gap.
proposals.edit: Keep the title, all three story lines and the question. Put the illustration in the right 45%; reflow the story on the left without reducing its type below the current readable size. If it crowds, use a reveal.
proposals.layout: Transparent 1536×1024 PNG with navy/teal continuity. Keep the complete artist and lantern scene. Use on white or the deck’s pale lavender; the navy-background preview shows weaker outline separation.
proposals.script: The artist wants to judge the revised prop in its surroundings. Bringing it into the engine serves that goal. What should update, and what surrounding work should remain stable?
proposals.limit: Generated concept art, not a before/after or evidence of reimport preservation. Raster only: no editable SVG master. Genuine alpha verified; original output has a maximum alpha of 254, which is retained.
proposals.title: User stories

proposals.heading: A prototype someone can actually operate
proposals.why: A photographed paper dropdown demonstrates how a sketch can simulate a choice. It is more informative than a polished illustration of people brainstorming.
proposals.edit: Keep this slide optional, its title and bullets. Replace the tiny sketch thumbnail with the full paper-dropdown photograph. Preserve the course’s two alternative layouts on live slide 32.
proposals.layout: Large 4:3 photo beside three short bullets. Do not crop away the hands or paper pieces: they explain the interaction. Keep the credit outside the image.
proposals.script: The paper pieces let a person make a choice. What could you learn from their attempt before implementing this control? What would still require a working tool?
proposals.limit: A browser-form prototype, not an Unreal interface. It can support discussion of interaction and labels, not execution correctness. No need to reproduce or distribute the downloadable template kit.
proposals.title: Sketching before implementation

proposals.heading: Selection, preview and visible scope in a real rename tool
proposals.why: The complete PowerRename window presents selection, original names, proposed names and Apply together. The task matches the renaming assessment more closely than generic UX stock imagery.
proposals.edit: Keep slide 34 optional. Offer this as an alternative to its production-menu example, not a second crowded image. Retain the distinction between filtering visible rows and changing the plan. The same source is a reference option for slide 52, but use it on only one slide.
proposals.layout: Full screenshot with its proportions unchanged; resize only under Microsoft’s screenshot terms. Point verbally to selection and the Original/Renamed columns. Do not crop or annotate its pixels.
proposals.script: Before Apply, which names will change? Which controls help you inspect that? Compare what you can see here with what you needed to know in the paper renamer case.
proposals.limit: Microsoft PowerToys PowerRename, a Windows file tool. Its preview is not evidence of backend stale-plan protection. It is also not an Unreal Actor renamer.
proposals.title: Mental models and visible scope

proposals.heading: A warning before an avoidable mistake
proposals.why: The missing-attachment warning offers a familiar example of noticing a likely problem before completing an action. It gives the class a quick comparison for actionable messages.
proposals.edit: Keep the course tool’s actual error screenshot as the main evidence. Add this as an optional reveal or companion link only if students need another example. Keep the existing recovery question.
proposals.layout: Full screenshot, large enough that the warning can be read; no decorative warning icons. If a small layout makes it illegible, leave it in the companion page.
proposals.script: What problem does this warning identify, and what can the person do next? Now read our tool’s message using those same questions.
proposals.limit: A separate email-product example published by NN/g, not a claim about the course tool. Preventing an error and recovering after a partial edit are different teaching cases.
proposals.title: An error should support recovery

proposals.heading: Show what visible focus actually means
proposals.why: The WAI figure gives “visible focus” an inspectable appearance. It fills a visual gap on a slide currently dominated by text and a short code excerpt.
proposals.edit: Keep the title, recovery qualifications and accessibility guidance. Add the intact WAI image alongside the focus sentence; keep its Draft status in the attribution. Preserve slide 56’s Qt-specific code as optional depth.
proposals.layout: Small supporting image at approximately its native 500-pixel width. Do not generatively upscale or remove the source’s annotation. Use an actual keyboard attempt in the course tool for behavior.
proposals.script: The outline identifies the active control. Can you tell where focus is in your own tool as you press Tab? A name in code is not enough to show that the experience works.
proposals.limit: A web example from a draft WAI teaching page. It demonstrates the idea; it does not certify desktop accessibility or show the course tool’s focus order.
proposals.title: Recovery and accessibility

proposals.heading: Recover the existing facilitator–task–participant diagram
proposals.why: Online checking led back to the NN/g role diagram already stored in the course. Final Class v2 removed it from this slide; it still matches the briefing directly.
proposals.edit: Keep the current three bullets and question. Reintroduce the existing diagram only if it remains legible at the available size; the roles in the course stay Author and Reviewer. Preserve the distinct follow-up photo on slide 45.
proposals.layout: Existing role diagram on the right; current lab-specific wording on the left. No new generated classroom scene. If the figure is crowded, retain the current plain briefing.
proposals.script: The author gives the goal and observes. The reviewer attempts it and records what happened. If help is needed, record that help. Which role or instruction needs clarification before we begin?
proposals.limit: The diagram is a general model. Our reciprocal classroom exercise and three reviewers are not a validated population-wide usability study.
proposals.title: Lab 2: three peer reviews

proposals.heading: Use the established Week 1 lenses only if they aid synthesis
proposals.why: The four existing badges offer stronger course continuity than another illustration. Their value is retrieval of familiar questions.
proposals.edit: Keep the current revision instructions and retest requirement. Optionally add a small, clearly labeled strip of original badges. Do not introduce a new rubric or add another discussion block.
proposals.layout: Original Constraints, Systems, Leverage and Throughput badges, unchanged. Labels remain editable. Prefer the current clean slide if the badges distract from writing the revision.
proposals.script: Which lens helps you explain your proposed revision? Choose one observed issue and state what you expect to see when you retest.
proposals.limit: Reuse, not a new online find. Artistic intent remains the goal examined through the lenses, not an added fifth lens.
proposals.title: One revision supported by evidence

rejections.title: Ryan DowlingSoka batch-renamer article
rejections.reason: Strong topic, weak new stills: the four inspected images are small parameters/Blueprint details, not a clear whole-tool preview. Already listed in the course references. Keep the tutorial link; do not inflate the screenshots.

rejections.title: Epic Interchange preview and conflicts
rejections.reason: Promising for slides 14 and 51, but three image downloads returned HTTP 403. Page descriptions were read; pixels were not inspected. Not counted as ready assets. Do not substitute a different importer UI or assert version compatibility.

rejections.title: Epic automatic reimport
rejections.reason: Settings screenshot and workflow explanation are useful references, but not a strong visual of an artist inspecting the revised prop.

rejections.title: Unreal Studio Reimport feature video
rejections.reason: Official 2018 Datasmith/Unreal Studio demonstration. Discovery and description checked, footage not inspected. Different workflow; not adopted as evidence for the current Python/import lesson.

rejections.title: Qt Designer tab-order screenshot
rejections.reason: Directly relevant to slide 56, but only 321×227 and visibly old styling. Keep as a linked optional reference. Do not upscale it into a main slide visual or confuse numbered design-time order with runtime focus.

rejections.title: Qt layout and signals documentation
rejections.reason: The inspected QFormLayout image is only 262×110. The generic signals diagram adds less than the current course-specific callback schematic. Qt documentation uses GFDL 1.3; software licensing is not the artwork license.

rejections.title: NN/g paper cutout alternatives
rejections.reason: Five photos inspected. Prefer the desktop dropdown for this artist-tool course. Phone cutouts, loading panels and overlays are less closely tied to the present teaching point.

rejections.title: NN/g error-image alternatives
rejections.reason: Five figures inspected. The print-area pair and attachment warning survive the relevance screen. Amazon checkout and password criteria add a larger domain detour.

rejections.title: PowerRename motion
rejections.reason: Two GIFs inspected through eight time samples each: 34.26-second rename sequence and 10.36-second filter sequence. The full still is easier to teach within the current budget. Motion remains linked from the publisher, not bundled as another live activity.

rejections.title: Epic Actor placement GIF
rejections.reason: 7.60-second drag-and-drop example inspected. Clear but less valuable than the material-override animation. It does not demonstrate reimport.

rejections.title: NN/g testing photograph
rejections.reason: The inspected 1400×933 photograph is already on slide 45 and depicts follow-up after a task. Do not reuse it as new evidence of silent observation during an attempt.

rejections.title: Guerrilla Horizon tools
rejections.reason: Strong existing source, already represented by production screenshots and a 16-second contextual-feedback clip. Keep those assets; do not count the source again as a new visual discovery.

rejections.title: Isaac Oster import/export
rejections.reason: Topic and author page confirmed through web reading; direct page retrieval returned HTTP 403. No newly inspected high-resolution still, so keep as study reference rather than pretending a clip was reviewed.

rejections.title: Generic UI/UX bottle, iceberg, maze and robot metaphors
rejections.reason: Rejected for this deck. They weaken the connection to actual tool scope, art decisions, and observed results. The newly found print-design example is more precise.
